Teleprompter Stories

Story library: 500 non-repeating generated stories for every grade level in each language. Story length, vocabulary, sentence structure, and reasoning demand increase independently from Grade 1 through Grade 12.
Struggling Reader Mode
No grade level. This is a struggling-reader track for learners who are still recognizing sounds and blending. Stories use short CVC words, simple names, and only a very small set of basic sight words. Advanced classroom words such as learner, lesson, and practice are excluded.
Language
Grade
Grade 7 • Junior High • 600–750 words
Longer informational or coming-of-age text with explicit reasoning, varied sentence structure, and more abstract ideas. Common themes: Adolescence, Self-Discovery, Friendship and Loyalty, Peer Pressure, Family Expectations, Courage, Acceptance, Conflict, Justice, Perseverance. Typical forms: Coming-of-Age, Realistic Fiction, Family & Peer Conflict, Justice Story, Informational Feature. Passage length follows the graded progression seen in the supplied Phil-IRI materials through the levels they cover; Grades 8–12 continue that progression with original, increasingly complex text. No Phil-IRI passage wording is copied.

About

Version v94

A focused classroom reading companion for guided practice and teacher monitoring.

Creator Jeromie Caballero
Facebook Instagram
How Fun Game Scoring Works One scoring system for Quick and One on 1
  1. Quick: Assess WORD DRILL only — 20 scored words: 10 Filipino and 10 English.
  2. One on 1: Assess WORD DRILL + PASSAGE. The passage depends on the learner's reading level.
  3. For every scored word, tap Very Good = 3, Good = 2, Fair = 1, or Meh = 0. Meh means the learner did not read the word.
  4. The highest score is 60 points (20 words × 3). The app changes the total into a percentage so Quick and One on 1 remain directly comparable.
  5. Reading remarks use the same cutoffs in both modes: 100% Best Reader, 80–99% Excellent, 70–79% Good, 50–69% Fair, and below 50% Remediation Is Needed.
  6. In One on 1, the extra pyramid/story is not given extra points. This keeps grading fair and uniform. The report still records that the check was One on 1 and identifies the added reading material.
Credits & References Reading references used in developing the app
Department of Education (DepEd) — ARAL-Reading BasicKS1 Tutor’s Guide – English; KS1 Tutor’s Guide – Filipino; KS2 Tutor’s Guide; KS3 Tutor’s Guide. Used for Key Stage, intervention-week, session, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension sequencing.
Department of Education (DepEd) — Phil-IRIPhil-IRI Full Package used as a reference for reading profiles, progression, passage calibration, and classroom reading assessment structure. App stories are not copies of Phil-IRI passages.
Marungko ApproachUnang Hakbang sa Pagbasa Gamit ang Marungko and Marungko Booklets 1–5 v.2 supplied with the project; TeachPinas-hosted reference copies were used to check lesson order and word focus.
Dolch Basic Sight VocabularyEdward William Dolch — reference basis for the Dolch/sight-word component.
Fry High-Frequency / Instant WordsEdward B. Fry — reference basis for high-frequency word practice.
Phonics and CVC banksTeacher-supplied word lists and app-curated real-word banks. CVC items are validated as consonant–vowel–consonant; phonics groups are kept pattern-specific and school-safe.

Reference materials are acknowledged for instructional alignment. The app is an independently developed classroom tool and does not claim ownership of DepEd, Phil-IRI, Marungko, Dolch, or Fry materials. Instructional note: Some learning materials in READING PAL are adapted, expanded, or teacher-developed to enrich lessons and provide extended practice for learners who need additional support. These supplemental materials are not official DepEd, Phil-IRI, or Marungko materials unless explicitly identified as such.

Aya's Turning Point

Aya entered a situation in the family dinner that seemed ordinary at first. A meeting record inside a cabinet later became a small but important detail. The tension began when friends pushed for a risky choice. A quiet choice at home affected what happened the next day. Friends expected a quick choice, but loyalty and honesty pulled in different directions. At home, a family expectation made the decision even harder. One person warned that refusing the group might lead to rejection. One friend admitted that peer pressure had shaped the first decision. Another friend argued that acceptance should not require doing what feels wrong. Aya asked what kind of person this choice would help them become. A difficult conversation exposed hurt feelings and corrected a rumor. The conflict did not disappear at once, but the conversation became more honest. The group still disagreed, but they stopped treating disagreement as betrayal. The final choice cost Aya some approval from others. That cost felt real, yet it also brought relief. Courage meant accepting a consequence instead of hiding from it. Later, a younger student asked what had happened. Aya explained the choice without pretending to be fearless. The experience made conflict a question of identity, choice, and courage. A close friend described how the choice could affect belonging. A younger student questioned whether popularity should decide what is right. A parent shared a different family expectation that changed the discussion. A teacher pointed out a consequence of staying silent. A community volunteer asked whose voice had not yet been heard.
